extracted.intended_audience: researchers in theoretical computer science and operations research (readers tracking P vs NP claims)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and heuristics for judging purported proofs or formulations (especially P vs NP and LP formulations of NP-hard problems), focusing on novelty, relation to known barriers, exposition clarity, and community validation. Useful for researchers deciding whether a claimed result merits deep investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamentally new approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper presents a fundamentally new approach or direction (bringing together disparate fields) rather than repeating previously tried methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post emphasizes that Deolalikar's paper used finite model theory to deduce structures in random satisfiability problems — a 'seriously and refreshingly new' idea that attracted top researchers' attention. Novelty of approach increases the chance experts will invest time in close scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why the approach evades known barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: The author must present reasons for believing the approach avoids known impossibility results and barrier arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: any method that cannot distinguish 2-SAT (easy) from 3-SAT (hard) is doomed; Yannakakis' results show symmetric LP formulations cannot capture NP-complete problems. A convincing paper should explicitly address such barriers and explain why it is not subject to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to distinguish easy vs hard instances (e.g., 2-SAT vs 3-SAT)
rubrics_metrics.description: The method must be capable of distinguishing problems known to differ in complexity (for example, distinguishing 2-satisfiability from 3-satisfiability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aaronson's blog and other commentators list this as a concrete check: if a proposed technique treats 2-SAT and 3-SAT indistinguishably, that is a strong sign the technique cannot succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with known problem structure / empirical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not conflict with what is already known about structures of problems (for example, random satisfiability problem structure in the critical region).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes that if P=NP then structures would have to be different than currently known; authors should relate new results to established structural knowledge and explain discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address symmetry/asymmetry requirements for LP formulations (Yannakakis barrier)
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims that linear programming formulations can capture NP-hard problems, the formulation must not be symmetric in the way Yannakakis disallows and must explain why its asymmetry avoids his proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct quote: 'Yannakakis showed that no symmetric formulation can do so... Not only must a formulation not be symmetric, but its asymmetry must be of the sort that continues to evade Yannakakis’ proof.' Authors need a strong argument for this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, usable exposition (avoid being merely a vague synopsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The presentation must be clear and detailed enough to be usable by readers and reviewers rather than vague high-level synopsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog criticizes a synopsis as 'vague to the point of not being usable.' Good exposition allows others to check the arguments and reproduce or critique details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness validated by knowledgeable experts / community scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: The correctness of a claimed result should be vetted by experts and the broader research community; widespread expert attention and detailed critiques are important signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post cites that many top mathematicians (Tao, Kalai, etc.) closely examined Deolalikar's paper and that detailed blog/wiki discussion (e.g., polymath wiki, Lipton, Aaronson) identified fundamental flaws. Community vetting via blogs, wikis, and direct expert review is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal acceptance alone is insufficient evidence of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication in a (third-tier) journal does not by itself make a controversial or surprising claim credible; community skepticism may remain even after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author observes that some papers were published in journals despite serious doubts and adds a step to the usual process: 'Your paper is accepted by a third tier journal and still no one believes it.' Prefer strong refereeing, high-quality venues, and community consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide concrete reasons and simpler proofs where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should clarify concepts and obtain simpler proofs of key claims when responding to criticism or revising work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deolalikar's revision claim included 'clarified some concepts; and obtained simpler proofs of several claims.' Offering clearer, simpler arguments helps others evaluate correctness and reduces the chance of overlooked flaws.
